summary: In a July 2026 proposed class complaint, Florida resident Tarra Chamberlain alleged that another participant manually ran Granola during at least one Microsoft Teams or Zoom meeting, causing her speech to be captured and transcribed without her knowledge or consent. She further alleged, on information and belief, that Granola used the meeting information to train its models. Granola describes a bot-free app that transcribes meeting audio, stores transcripts rather than recordings, and uses anonymised data for its own model improvement unless an account user opts out; Enterprise training is off by default. A non-user participant lacks that account setting. The filing and product posture are established, but the particular meeting’s permissions, actual inclusion of her data in training, and lawsuit outcome are not.

assessment_boundaries: The complaint alleges capture and training use; the docket establishes filing but no merits determination.
Granola’s security page describes a generic processing posture, not event-level evidence about Chamberlain’s meeting.
The separate report about link sharing is contextual and does not establish disclosure of Chamberlain’s notes.
vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The original Chamberlain complaint says she participated in at least one Teams or Zoom meeting from Florida, was unaware Granola was present, and had her communications intercepted and transcribed. It alleges training use on information and belief, not a traced sample-to-model lineage. The court docket confirms filing but does not report a merits finding. Granola’s own security page says users must manually start the bot-free app; it accesses computer meeting audio, transcribes it, stores transcript/notes rather than meeting audio, and trains on anonymised data for improvement unless an account holder opts out; Enterprise is off by default. Thus a generic secondary-purpose capability and asymmetry for non-users are provider-reported, while any actual inclusion of Chamberlain’s utterances, account plan, opt-out state and meeting notice remain unproved. The separate Verge report about link sharing is a contextual platform concern, not evidence her notes were shared.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The complaint describes two distinct questions: whether another attendee’s use of Granola authorised transcription of Chamberlain’s contribution, and whether any captured material was reused for model improvement. Granola’s policy and product design make both pathways relevant, but the complaint does not prove participant-level notice or consent, account-plan or opt-out state, or inclusion of Chamberlain’s data in training. Both findings remain unresolved. Transcription and possible model-improvement reuse remain distinct unresolved claims. Plan, notice, opt-out and actual training inclusion are unknown; a non-user’s lack of an account setting does not prove the secondary processing event. The independent privacy and autonomy assessment is Boundary. The decisive participant-level permission and processing evidence is not available. The Granola claim materially engages acquisition of private meeting speech. The preserved pleading identifies the claimed capture and lack of consent, but does not resolve the actual meeting-specific notice, permission and capture record. Neither unauthorised acquisition nor verified authorised confinement is established.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: Unlike bot-joining systems, this application can capture meeting audio from a participant’s device without joining the call. The governance question still concerns all affected speakers, not the visual presence of a bot. Provider policy supports a secondary training-purpose posture, while the actual plaintiff-specific use requires further evidence.
